Name and describe the five data types in the specification and give an example of each. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

A data type tells the computer what kind of data an item is, for example a whole number, a date or some text. Data must be defined as a particular type before it is processed. This matters for three main reasons. First, it decides what processing is possible: numbers can be added and averaged, dates can be put in order or used to work out how many days are left, and text can be searched or joined together.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Second, it helps the computer store data efficiently, because each type is stored in a particular way. Third, it supports validation. If a field is set to integer, a type check will reject an entry such as 'twelve', which helps stop errors getting into the system. Choosing the right type when a database, spreadsheet or program is set up saves problems later.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Numeric data is data that you can do calculations with. The specification splits it into two types. An integer is a whole number with no decimal or fractional part. It can be positive or negative, so 28, 0 and -4 are all integers. Integers suit counts, such as the number of pupils in a class, tickets sold for a school show or a score of 51 in a test.
Got it. Keep going.

A real number can have a decimal or fractional part, such as 1.62, 3.99 or -4.6. Real numbers can also be positive or negative, and the set of real numbers includes whole numbers too. Real is used for measurements and money, such as heights, temperatures and prices. In C sharp, the course programming language, int stores integers and double stores real numbers. In a database, money is often stored using a currency type, which is shown with a currency symbol and two decimal places.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

The date/time type stores dates, times or both. Because the computer knows the value is a date, it can sort records by date and calculate with them, such as finding everyone whose membership ends this month. Date/time also controls how the value is displayed. Software offers ready-made formats, for example a long date (Saturday, 12 September 2026), a medium date (12-Sep-2026) or a short date (12/09/2026), and similar long, medium and short time formats; users can also create their own. A character is one single letter, digit or symbol, such as a grade 'B' or 'Y' for yes.
Okay. Keep going.

It is stored using its code from the character set, such as ASCII. A string is a sequence of characters, such as a name, address or postcode. Strings can vary in length. Any digits in a string are treated as text, so they cannot be used in calculations.
Go on.

Many exam questions give you an item of data and ask for the most suitable type and a reason. Work through a few questions in order. Will calculations be done with it? If so it is numeric: real if it needs a decimal part, integer if not. Is it a date or time? Then use date/time. Is it always exactly one character?
Right. Keep going.

Then character. Everything else is a string. Watch for 'numbers' that are really text. A mobile phone number such as 07700 900123 must be a string, because storing it as an integer would remove the leading zero, the space would not be allowed and nobody ever adds phone numbers together. Postcodes such as BT92 1AB mix letters and digits, so they are strings too. A pupil's age is an integer, but their date of birth is date/time, because the age can be worked out from it and it stays correct as time passes.

Data type?
The kind of data an item is (such as integer, real, date/time, character or string), which decides how it is stored and processed.
Integer?
Data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, with no decimal or fractional part.
Real?
Data type for numbers that can have a decimal or fractional part, positive or negative. Real numbers also include whole numbers.
Date/time?
Data type that stores dates and/or times so that they can be sorted, calculated with and shown in different formats.
Character?
Data type for a single letter, digit or symbol, stored using its code from the character set.
String or text?
Data type for a sequence of characters (letters, digits and symbols) of variable length.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Data types come up in most Unit 1 papers, often worth one mark per item. You may be asked to match sample values to data types, choose types for database fields or justify a choice. In the 2023 paper, question 1 the data types question was part of a short-answer question on data. A 'state' question needs just the type name. A 'describe' question needs what the type stores plus an example, for example 'Real stores numbers with a decimal part, such as a price of 2.85'. A justification must link to the data itself. Saying 'because it is a number' will not earn the mark; 'because it is a whole number used to count pupils' will. In database questions, Access names such as Currency, Short Text or Yes/No are also credited. The most frequent lost marks come from calling a phone number an integer.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Why is a mobile phone number not stored as an integer? Is it A, It is too long to store; B, Integers cannot be sorted; C, It uses less storage; D, The leading zero would be lost?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is D: The leading zero would be lost. Integers drop leading zeros, so 07700 900123 would become 7700900123. Phone numbers are also never used in calculations.
